This species displays a clear size gradient across its life history; field surveys indicate that the ultimate total length attained by adults is 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], representing the maximum recorded size for the population. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of large adults was estimated at 1300 grams [Wwi = 1300 grams] using allometric scaling relationships derived from local catch data. These morphological extremes are seldom achieved, as most individuals succumb to natural mortality or fishing pressure well before reaching such dimensions.

Sexual maturation in female Epinephelus rivulatus occurs at a relatively modest body size compared to the species’ asymptotic length. Histological examination of ovarian tissue revealed that the total length at puberty for females is 19.4 centimeters [Lp = 19.4 centimeters]. The corresponding wet weight at this developmental milestone was calculated to be 100.5 grams [Wwp = 100.5 grams], based on length-weight regressions parameterized for this serranid. This pubertal mass is several orders of magnitude greater than the mass at birth, since females begin life as minute pelagic larvae. The ontogenetic transition from a larval existence to a demersal juvenile stage involves profound morphological transformation and a substantial increase in body mass over the first few months following settlement.

Spawning events for this species produce large numbers of small, pelagic eggs that undergo external fertilisation in the water column. The fertilised ovum, a yolk-laden sphere with a diameter of approximately 0.6 millimeters, develops rapidly before the larva emerges. At the moment of eclosion, the newly hatched yolk-sac larva has a wet weight of roughly 0.000113 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.000113 grams], reflecting the modest energetic reserves packaged into each egg. This lecithotrophic stage is brief, as the prolarva must quickly transition to exogenous feeding once the yolk reserves are depleted. The survival of these delicate, free-swimming larvae is strongly influenced by the availability of suitable zooplankton prey during the critical period following mouth opening and first feeding.

Longevity records for Epinephelus rivulatus were derived from annual growth increments observed in sagittal otoliths, which offered a robust means of age determination for individuals collected across the species’ range. The maximum documented lifespan, based on these otolith readings, was calculated to be 2555 days [am = 2555 days] under the prevailing thermal regime of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to approximately seven years, is consistent with the moderate generation times reported for other protogynous serranids of comparable adult body size. Age-related mortality appears to accelerate after the fifth year, with very few individuals surviving beyond the sixth annual spawning season. The oldest captured specimens exhibited signs of reproductive senescence and reduced condition factor.

Comparisons with congeneric species reveal that Epinephelus rivulatus occupies an intermediate position in terms of both body size and reproductive timing. While some larger groupers may exceed 100 centimeters in ultimate length, the 45 centimeter [Li = 45 centimeter] asymptotic length recorded here aligns with the typical dimensions of small-to-medium bodied serranids inhabiting subtropical reef systems. The mass at puberty, documented at just over one hundred grams [Wwp = one hundred grams], is reached relatively early in the lifespan, enabling females to contribute to the spawning stock for several consecutive seasons.
